1. Getting started

Source: vignettes/bayclumpr.Rmd
bayclumpr.Rmd

bayclumpr fits calibrations between clumped isotopes (D47) and temperature. It then uses these calibrations to reconstruct temperatures for new samples. You can fit calibrations under frequentist and Bayesian frameworks. The same functions run BayClump, a Shiny app that you can use from your browser.

This vignette covers the data you need and a first example. The other vignettes go into more detail:

  1. Getting started (this vignette).
  2. vignette("frequentist", package = "bayclumpr"): OLS, weighted OLS, Deming, and York regressions.
  3. vignette("bayesian", package = "bayclumpr"): Bayesian calibrations, priors, model comparison, and reconstructions.
  4. vignette("covariates", package = "bayclumpr"): Bayesian calibrations with a second predictor.
  5. vignette("comparison", package = "bayclumpr"): frequentist and Bayesian approaches on the same dataset, with plots of parameters and reconstructions.
library(bayclumpr)

The workflow

Every analysis has two steps. First, we fit a calibration. The result is a table with many plausible values of the intercept (alpha), the slope (beta), and the scatter around the calibration line (sigma). Second, we use that table to reconstruct temperatures for new samples. Frequentist functions get these values by bootstrapping. Bayesian functions get them from the posterior distribution.

Step Frequentist Bayesian
1. Calibrate cal.ols(), cal.wols(), cal.deming(), cal.york() cal.bayesian(), cal.ion.bayesian()
2. Get the table of alpha, beta, and sigma Returned by the functions above cal.draws()
3. Reconstruct rec.clumped() rec.bayesian(), rec.ion.bayesian()

Preparing your data

Calibration data

Calibration datasets need the following columns:

Column Description
Temperature Temperature as 106/T2, with T in kelvin
TempError Uncertainty in Temperature (1 SD, in the same units)
D47 Measured D47
D47error Uncertainty in D47 (1 SD)
Material Material of each sample. Only needed for mixed models

All uncertainties are 1 SD of the value in the table. If D47 is the mean of several replicates, D47error should be the standard error of that mean. The same applies to TempError.

Converting temperatures

Temperatures are often reported in °C. temp2x() converts them to 106/T2 and propagates their errors. The result has the column names that the calibration functions expect:

temp2x(c(5, 25, 50), tempError = c(0.5, 0.5, 1))
#>   Temperature  TempError
#> 1   12.925337 0.04646894
#> 2   11.249426 0.03773076
#> 3    9.576166 0.05926762

x2temp() converts them back to °C.

Averaging replicates

When each sample has several replicate measurements, avg.replicates() averages them and returns the standard error of each mean as D47error:

reps <- data.frame(
  Sample = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3),
  D47 = c(0.601, 0.598, 0.605, 0.702, 0.695, 0.699),
  Material = "calcite"
)
avg.replicates(reps)
#>   Sample       D47       D47sd N    D47error Material
#> 1      A 0.6013333 0.003511885 3 0.002027588  calcite
#> 2      B 0.6986667 0.003511885 3 0.002027588  calcite

By default, the SE comes from the SD of each sample’s replicates. With few replicates, this SD is poorly constrained. The pooledSD argument uses a common SD instead, such as the long-term SD of standards measured in the same lab.

Reconstruction data

Reconstruction datasets need Sample, D47, and D47error. Mixed models also need Material, with the same labels used in the calibration.

Simulated data

cal.dataset() simulates calibration datasets with known parameters (alpha = 0.268 and beta = 0.0369). There are three error scenarios: low ("S1"), intermediate ("S2"), and high ("S3"). The columns x_TRUE and y_TRUE hold the true values before measurement error.

set.seed(3)
ds <- cal.dataset(error = "S1", nobs = 50)
head(ds)
#>      x_TRUE Temperature TempError    y_TRUE D47error       D47 Material
#> 1 10.076133   10.089943     0.019 0.6475262   0.0025 0.6442978        1
#> 2 11.414949   11.399569     0.019 0.6841481   0.0025 0.6907357        1
#> 3 12.517576   12.522651     0.019 0.7430624   0.0025 0.7442800        1
#> 4  9.695736    9.662728     0.019 0.6333012   0.0025 0.6354360        1
#> 5 12.391566   12.364749     0.019 0.7379670   0.0025 0.7406881        1
#> 6 12.060248   12.051630     0.019 0.7206252   0.0025 0.7211903        1

A first example

We fit an OLS calibration with 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Each row of the result is one replicate.

ols <- cal.ols(data = ds, replicates = 1000)
head(ols)
#>       alpha       beta      sigma
#> 1 0.2551112 0.03805364 0.01270688
#> 2 0.2645517 0.03720573 0.01338969
#> 3 0.2739421 0.03638998 0.01147219
#> 4 0.2675038 0.03681503 0.01205161
#> 5 0.2896745 0.03498087 0.01064595
#> 6 0.2682990 0.03664613 0.01425720

cal.summary() summarizes any calibration in the same way:

cal.summary(ols)
#>   parameter   estimate           SE     median      lower      upper
#> 1     alpha 0.27022607 0.0106035367 0.27029091 0.24894691 0.29123768
#> 2      beta 0.03660694 0.0009469391 0.03662508 0.03469022 0.03850465
#> 3     sigma 0.01298611 0.0011871156 0.01299158 0.01067024 0.01526967

estimate is the mean of each parameter and SE is its standard error, which is the SD of the bootstrap replicates. sigma is itself an SD: the scatter of individual samples around the calibration line.

Next, we create a reconstruction dataset for three samples, each measured three times, and reconstruct their temperatures:

recData <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Sample 1", "Sample 2", "Sample 3"),
  D47 = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8),
  D47error = 0.006,
  N = 3
)

rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = ols)
#>     Sample D47 D47error  meanTemp       SD       SE    median     lower
#> 1 Sample 1 0.6    0.006  60.02587 5.451499 3.329676  59.99816  53.70975
#> 2 Sample 2 0.7    0.006  18.70133 3.574933 2.155759  18.68351  14.60380
#> 3 Sample 3 0.8    0.006 -10.28279 2.761595 1.739932 -10.27637 -13.73321
#>       upper
#> 1 66.796937
#> 2 23.005687
#> 3 -6.900347

All temperatures are in °C. meanTemp is the temperature from the mean slope and intercept. SE is the standard error of the temperature, based on D47error, the standard error of the mean D47. SD is the uncertainty of the temperature of a single replicate, based on the SD of the replicates (D47error × sqrt(N)). Both include the uncertainty in the calibration. SD is NA when the dataset has neither N nor D47sd.

median, lower, and upper are the median and the limits of the 95% interval, based on SE. Temperature is a nonlinear function of D47, so the interval is not symmetric around the median.

From here, vignette("frequentist", package = "bayclumpr") compares the four frequentist models. vignette("bayesian", package = "bayclumpr") shows the same workflow under a Bayesian framework.
